Some of them said: it is superfluous, and its superfluity is found in the speech of the Arabs, as in His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate," and ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I remembered Layla, and passion seized me,*
*and the core of my heart almost was cut, not cut.*

Others said: it is a rejection of their speech, in which they denied the resurrection, as if he said: "The matter is not as you mention. [I swear by the Day of Resurrection]." This is the view of al-Farra' and many of the grammarians, like the saying of one speaker: "No, by God," so *la* is a rejection of a statement that preceded it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*No, by your father, daughter of al-ʿAmiri,*
*the people do not claim that I flee.*

It was also said that it is for negation, but not a negation of the oath itself; rather, it negates what indicates the magnification and exaltation of the one sworn by. As if the meaning of "la uqsimu bi-kadhā" (I do not swear by such-and-such) is: I do not magnify it by swearing by it as it deserves to be magnified, for it deserves more than that.

It was also said that it is for negating the oath because the matter is clear. The discussion of this has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿So I do not swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 75].

Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir in one narration from him, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Hurmuz read *la-uqsimu* without the alif, on the basis that the *lam* is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). The first view is the most preferred of these views. Al-Razi objected to it with things that do not weaken its strength nor undermine its preponderance. God's swearing by the Day of Resurrection is for its glorification and exaltation, and God may swear by whatever of His creatures He wills.

﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾. Some people went to the view that He, glory be to Him, swore by the self-reproaching soul just as He swore by the Day of Resurrection, so the discussion about this *la* is like the discussion about the first one. This is the view of the majority.

Al-Hasan said: He swore by the Day of Resurrection and did not swear by the self-reproaching soul.

Al-Tha'labi said: The correct view is that He swore by both of them together. The meaning of "the self-reproaching soul" is the soul that blames its owner for his shortcoming, or that blames all souls for their shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: By God, it is the soul of the believer. You do not see the believer except that he blames himself: "What did I intend by such-and-such? What did I intend by such-and-such?" But the wicked does not rebuke his soul.

Mujahid said: It is the soul that blames for what has passed and regrets. It blames itself for evil: why did it do it? And for good: why did it not increase it? Al-Farra' said: There is no soul, whether righteous or wicked, except that it blames itself. If it has done good, it says: "If only I had done more." If it has done evil, it says: "If only I had not done it."

On this basis, the speech is coming in the manner of praise for the soul, so swearing by it is good and permissible.

It was also said that *al-lawwama* means "the one who is blamed and disgraced," so it is a description of blame. On this basis, whoever denied that it is an oath argued, since the soul of the disobedient has no worth by which one would swear.

Muqatil said: It is the soul of the unbeliever, which blames itself and grieves in the Hereafter over what it neglected regarding God's right. The first is preferable.

﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ The intended meaning of "man" is the species. It was said that "man" means the unbeliever. The *hamza* is for denial. *An* is the lightened form of the heavy (*an*), and its noun is a deleted pronoun of the matter. The meaning: Does man think that the matter is that We will not gather his bones after they have become dust, so that We would restore them as a new creation? That is a false supposition, for We gather them. What this statement indicates is the answer to the oath.

Al-Zajjaj said: I swear by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul that We will surely gather the bones for resurrection. This is the answer to the oath.

Al-Nahhas said: The answer to the oath is omitted, meaning: "He will surely resurrect," and the meaning is that God, glory be to Him, resurrects all the parts of man. He specified the bones because they are the mold of creation.

﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾. *Bala* is an affirmation of what follows the negation to which the interrogation is directed. Pausing on this word is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His saying *qadirina* (able). The accusative of *qadirina* is in the status of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Yes, We gather them, being able." So the state is from the implied verb's pronoun. It was also said the meaning is: "Yes, We gather them, estimating [ourselves] able."

Al-Farra' said: That is, We are able, and We are capable of more than that.

He also said: It is permissible to put it in the accusative by repetition, meaning: "Yes, let him reckon us able." It was also said the estimate is: "Yes, We were able."

Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *bala qadirun* (yes, [We] are able), on the estimate of a subject: that is, "Yes, We are able."

The meaning of ﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾ is: to join some of them to others, and return them as they were, despite their fineness and smallness. How then [would it be] with the large limbs? God, glory be to Him, drew attention with the *banan*, which is the fingers, to the rest of the limbs, and that the power to resurrect them and return them as they were is more fitting in power than returning the small, delicate fingers, which contain joints, nails, delicate veins, and fine bones. This is the reason for specifying them by mention. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba said this.

Most of the exegetes said: The meaning of the verse is that We would make the fingers of his hands and feet one thing, like the sole of a camel or the hoof of a donkey, a single plate without cracks in it, so he would not be able to benefit from them in delicate work such as writing, sewing, and the like. But We separated his fingers so that he may benefit by them.

It was also said the meaning is: Rather, We are able to return man in the form of beasts, so how much more in the form in which he was? The first is preferable. From it is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Death is subject to my hand, when I*
*join its fingertips with the Hindi sword.*

By *banan* he drew attention to the rest of the limbs.

﴿Rather, man desires to continue in sin ahead of him﴾. This is coordinated with "Does man think" either as an interrogation similar to it, turning away from the rebuke by that to the rebuke by this, or as an affirmation which has moved from interrogation.

The meaning: Rather, man desires to advance his wickedness among the times before him, and what time will come to him, so he advances the sin and delays repentance.

Ibn al-Anbari said: He desires to commit wickedness for as long as his life is extended, and it is not in his intention to turn back from a sin that he commits.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He says, "I will repent later," and does not repent until death comes to him while he is in his worst condition.

Al-Dahhak said: It is hope. He says, "I will live and enjoy some of the world," and does not mention death. *Fujur* (wickedness) originally means inclination away from the truth. It applies to everyone who inclines from the truth by speech or action. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He swore by God, Abu Hafs ʿUmar,*
*that no thorn-prick or thorn-scratch touched her. O God, forgive him if he was wicked.*

﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This sentence is a new statement explaining the meaning of "yafjur" (continues in sin). The meaning: he asks when the Day of Resurrection is, by way of asking with disbelief and mockery.

﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. That is: it is terrified and bewildered. From "barraqa al-rajul," when a man looks at lightning and his sight is stunned.

The majority read *bariqa* with a kasra on the *ra'*.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and al-Zajjaj and others said: the meaning is "bewildered, so he does not blink." From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Even if Luqman the wise were confronted*
*by a clear Mayy [a woman] before his eyes, he would almost be dazzled.*

Al-Khalil and al-Farra' said: *bariqa* with a kasra means: terrified, stunned, and bewildered. The Arabs say of the astonished person: "He has become *bariq*, so he is *bariq*." Al-Farra' recited:

*Tend your soul and do not weary me,*
*treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

That is: do not be terrified by the multitude of wounds that are on you.

Nafiʿ and Aban on the authority of ʿAsim read *baraqa* with a fatha on the *ra'*: that is, his sight shone from the intensity of its staring at death.

Mujahid and others said: This is at the time of death. It was said: *baraqa*, *yabraqu*, means he split his eyes open and kept them open.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The fatha and the kasra of the *ra'* are two dialects with the same meaning.

﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾. The majority read *khasafa* with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *sin*, in the active voice.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, and Abu Haywah read it with a damma on the *kha'* and a kasra on the *sin*, in the passive voice. The meaning of "khasafa al-qamar": its light has gone and does not return, as it returns when it is eclipsed in this world. It is said *khasafa* when all its light has gone, and *kasafa* when some of its light has gone.

﴿And the sun and moon are joined﴾: that is, their light has gone entirely. He did not say "joined" (feminine), because the feminine is metaphorical. Al-Mubarrad said this.

Abu ʿUbayda said: It is the predominance of the masculine over the feminine.

Al-Kisa'i said: It is treated according to the meaning of a collection of lights.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: He did not say "jumiʿat" because the meaning between them is in the going of their light. It was also said: He joined them in their rising from the west, both black, folded, and dark.

ʿAta' said: He will join them on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be thrown into the sea and become the great fire of God.

It was also said: The sun and the moon will be joined, so there will be no alternation of night and day there.

Ibn Masʿud read: "And the sun and the moon were joined."

﴿On that day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ That is: he says at the occurrence of these events, "Where is the escape?" *Al-mafarr* is a verbal noun in the sense of *al-firar* (flight).

Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that it is the place of flight. From it is the saying of the poet:

*Where is the escape, while the rams butt each other,*
*and every ram that flees from them is disgraced?*

Al-Mawardi said: It admits two meanings: first, where is the escape from God, glory be to Him, out of shame before Him? Second, where is the escape from Hell, out of fear of it?

The majority read ﴿ayna al-mafarr﴾ with a fatha on the *mim* and the *fa'*, as a verbal noun, as has already passed.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'*, as a noun of place: that is, where is the place of flight?

Al-Kisa'i said: They are two dialects, like *madabb* and *midabb*, and *masahh* and *misahh*. al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa'*, meaning by it the man who is good at fleeing. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Attacking, fleeing, advancing, retreating, together, like a boulder of rock that the torrent has cast down from a height.*

That is: good at fleeing and attacking.

﴿Never! There is no refuge﴾. That is: there is no mountain, no fortress, and no shelter from God.

Ibn Jubayr said: there is no escape and no protection.

*Al-wazar* in language is what a person takes refuge in: a fortress, a mountain, or other things. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*Bakr surely knows that we are the best in judgment and in the moment of fear, a refuge.*

Another said:

*By my life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age.*

Al-Suddi said: When they were frightened in the world they would take refuge in the mountains. So God said to them: "There is no refuge that will protect you from Me on that day." And *kalla* (never) is for rebuke, or for negating what preceded it, or with the meaning of "truly."

﴿To your Lord on that day is the resting place﴾. That is: the return, the end, and the destination, not to anything else. It was also said: To Him is the judgment among the servants, not to anything else. It was also said: *al-mustaqarr* is the settling where God settles them.

﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind﴾. That is: on the Day of Resurrection he will be informed of what good and evil he did.

Qatadah said: of the obedience he did, and the obedience he left and did not do.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: of what he sent ahead of his wealth and what he left to the heirs.

Mujahid said: of the first of his deeds and the last of them.

Al-Dahhak said: of the obligation he sent ahead and the obligation he left.

Al-Qushayri said: This informing will be on the Day of Resurrection at the weighing of deeds, and it may be at the time of death.

Al-Qurtubi said: The first is more apparent.

﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾. The *basirah* (witness, insight) is raised as the predicate of *al-insan*. *ʿAla nafsihi* (against himself) is connected to *basirah*.

Al-Akhfash said: He made it [the human being] himself the insight (baṣīrah), just as you say of a man, "You are a proof against yourself." It was also said that the meaning is that his limbs bear witness against him for what he did, as in His words: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. Al-Farra' recited:

*As if upon the man of intellect there is an eye that sees,*
*Observing his place, or a watcher who is looking.*

So the meaning is: rather, the human's limbs are witnesses against him.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Qutaybi said: This *hā'* in *baṣīrah* is what the grammarians call the *hā' al-mubālaghah* (the *hā'* of intensification), as in their saying *'allāmah* (very learned).

It was also said that *al-baṣīrah* refers to the two recording angels who write down whatever good and evil he does, and the *tā'* in that case is the feminine marker.

Al-Hasan said: That is, he is perceptive of the faults of his own self.

﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: that is, even if he makes excuses and argues on behalf of himself, that will not benefit him.

It is said *ma'dhirah* and *ma'ādhir* (pl.).

Al-Farra' said: That is, even if he makes excuses, there will be someone to deny his excuse.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ma'ādhir* means the veils (*al-sutūr*), and its singular is *mi'dhār*. That is: even if he lets down veils, wishing to hide himself, his own self is a witness against him. Thus said al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddi, and the veil in the dialect of Yemen is called *mi'dhār*. Thus said al-Mubarrad, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*But she [the dwelling] withheld for a while a place from us,*
*And she spent her day with veils (al-ma'ādhir).*

The first interpretation is the better one, and it was the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil. Similar to it is His words: ﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ [Ghafir: 52], and His words: ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], and the saying of the poet:

*It is not good that a man should excuse himself,*
*When among all the people there is no one to excuse him.*

﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to move his lips and tongue with the Qur'an when it was revealed to him, before Jibril had finished reciting the revelation, out of eagerness to memorize it (ﷺ). So this verse was revealed: that is, do not move your tongue with the Qur'an when the revelation is being delivered, in order to take it quickly, fearing that it might slip away from you. Similar to this is His words: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], and so on.

﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection﴾ in your breast, so that nothing of it is lost to you, ﴿and its recitation﴾, that is, the establishing of its recitation on your tongue.

Al-Farra' said: *al-qirā'ah* and *al-Qur'ān* are both verbal nouns (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: ﴿So follow its recitation﴾ means: follow its laws and rulings.

﴿So when We have recited it﴾, that is, when We have completed its recitation to you through the tongue of Jibril, ﴿then follow its recitation﴾, that is, its recitation.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾, that is, the explanation of what it contains of the lawful and the unlawful, and the clarifying of what is unclear in it.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that upon Us is that We send it down to you as an Arabic Qur'an, containing clarification for the people.

It was also said that the meaning is: indeed, it is upon Us that We make it clear through your tongue.

﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾. (*Kallā*) is for deterring from haste and for encouraging patience. It was also said that it is a deterrence for those who do not believe in the Qur'an and in its being clear, from among the disbelievers.

'Ata' said: That is, Abu Jahl does not believe in the Qur'an and its clarification.

The people of Medina and the Kufans recited ﴿Rather, you love﴾ and *tadharūna* (you leave) with the second-person form in both verbs. The rest recited with the third-person form in both. According to the first reading, the address is to them as rebuke and reproach. According to the second reading, the speech refers back to the human being, since it means "people." The meaning is: you love the world and leave the Hereafter, so you do not act for it.

﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾, that is, bright, fresh and beautiful. It is said: a tree that is *nāḍir* and a meadow that is *nāḍir*, meaning beautiful and luxuriant. The freshness of life is its beauty and delight.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators say: shining, luminous, bright.

﴿Looking at their Lord﴾. This is from looking (*naẓar*): that is, to their Creator and the Owner of their affair. *Nāẓirah*: that is, they look at Him. This is what the majority of the scholars said. What is meant by it is what the sound hadiths have transmitted in a widely transmitted way (*mutawātir*), that the servants will look upon their Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as they look at the moon on the night of the full moon.

Ibn Kathir said: And this, praise be to Allah, is agreed upon among the Companions, the Successors and the predecessors of this Ummah, just as it is agreed upon among the Imams of Islam and the guides of mankind.

Mujahid said: Here *naẓar* means waiting for the reward that they have with Allah. Something similar was narrated from 'Ikrimah.

It was said: this is not authentically reported except from Mujahid alone.

When someone says, "I looked at so-and-so," it is nothing but seeing with the eye. When they want to mean waiting, they say *naẓartuhu* (I awaited him), as in the words of the poet:

*Indeed, if you two would wait for me (tunẓirānī) for a while of time,*
*It would benefit me before Umm Jundab.*

When they want the sight of the eye, they say *naẓartu ilayhi* (I looked at him), as the poet said:

*I looked at her while the stars were like*
*Lamps of monks kindled for a feast.*

And the saying of another:

*Indeed I, when you promised me, am looking (nāẓir) to you*
*With the look of the poor man at the wealthy rich one.*

That is: I look at you with the look of humility, as the poor man looks at the rich man. The poetry and sayings of the Arabs on this are very numerous.

*Wujūh* (faces) is the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible to begin with it though it is indefinite, because the context is one of detailing. *Nāḍirah* is an adjective of *wujūh*, and *yawma'idhin* (on that day) is an adverbial complement of *nāḍirah*. Even if the context were not one of detailing, the description of the indefinite by the phrase *nāḍirah* would make it permissible to begin with it. But the context of detailing by itself permits beginning with an indefinite noun.

﴿And faces on that Day will be gloomy﴾, that is, frowning, scowling, dejected.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: *basara al-rajul wajhahu busūran*, meaning he frowned.

Al-Suddi said: *bāsirah* means changed, and it was said: yellowed. The faces here refer to the faces of the disbelievers.

﴿They will think that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾. *Al-fāqirah* is the great catastrophe. It is said: *faqarahu al-fāqirah*, meaning it broke his spine.

Qatadah said: *al-fāqirah* is evil. Al-Suddi said: destruction. Ibn Zayd said: entering the Fire.

The origin of *al-fāqirah* is branding on the nose of a camel with an iron or fire until it reaches the bone. Thus said al-Asma'i. From this comes their saying, "He has worked on him the *fāqirah*."

Al-Nabighah said:

*Is there for me a grave that always stands before me,*
*And a blow of an axe above my head, a *fāqirah*?*

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His words: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1]. He said: Your Lord swears by whatever of His creation He wills. I said: ﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 2]. He said: the blameworthy self (*al-nafs al-la'ūm*). I said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3] ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 4]. He said: If He willed, He would make it a hoof or a claw.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: *al-lawwāmah* (the self-reproaching) means the blameworthy.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also: it is the one that blames for good and evil, saying, "If only I had done such and such."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also: it regrets what has passed and blames itself for it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also regarding ﴿But man wishes to continue in sin before him﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 5]: he said: it proceeds forward.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding the verse: he said: he is the disbeliever who denies the reckoning.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: he said: that is, the hope (*al-amal*). He says: I will act, then repent.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Amal* and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from him also regarding the verse: he said: he puts off repentance and delays it.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, (p. 1560) and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from him also: ﴿But man wishes to continue in sin before him﴾ he says: "I will repent later." ﴿He asks: when is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 6]. He said: he says, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" He said: So He explained to him: ﴿When the sight is dazzled﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 7]. Ibn Jarir transmitted from him: when the sight is dazzled, meaning death.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿No refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11]: he said: no fortress.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas through several chains regarding His words: ﴿No refuge﴾: he said: no fortress and no refuge. In one wording: no protection. In another wording: no mountain.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and kept back﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]: he said: what he sent forward of deeds, and what he kept back of a sunnah practiced after him, whether good or evil.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similar from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: what he sent forward of disobedience and what he kept back of obedience, and he will be informed of that.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through several chains from him regarding His words: ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 14]: he said: he bears witness against himself alone. ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: he said: even if he makes excuses.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾: he said: his hearing, his sight, his hands, his feet and his limbs. ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: he said: even if he strips off his clothes.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to suffer hardship in receiving the revelation, so he would move his tongue and lips with it, fearing that it would slip away from him, desiring to memorize it. So Allah revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17]. He said: It says: indeed upon Us is that We gather it in your breast, then you recite it. ﴿So when We have recited it﴾: it says: when We have sent it down to you. ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾: listen to it and be silent. ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾: that We explain it through your tongue. In another wording: upon Us is that We recite it. So after that, whenever Jibril came to him, he would lower his gaze (in another wording: listen), and when he left, he would recite it, just as Allah had promised him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: ﴿So when We have recited it﴾: he said: We have clarified it. ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾: he says: act upon it. 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾: he said: the world was hastened for them, its evil and its good, and the Hereafter was hidden from them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾: he said: luxuriant.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ajurri in *al-Shari'ah*, al-Lalika'i in *al-Sunnah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ru'yah* transmitted from him regarding ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾: he said: meaning their beauty. ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾: he said: they looked at the Creator.

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him: ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾: he said: they look at the face of their Lord.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas ibn Malik who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾ ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾, he said: They will look at their Lord without modality, without a bounded limit, and without a known attribute."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The people said: O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection? He said: Do you have any difficulty seeing the sun when there is no cloud beneath it? They said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said: Do you have any difficulty seeing the moon on the night of the full moon when there is no cloud beneath it? They said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said: Indeed you will see Him on the Day of Resurrection in the same way."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah.

We have already mentioned that the hadiths about the vision are widely transmitted, so we will not lengthen by citing them; they come in a separate work. Those who denied it and considered it far-fetched have not held onto anything that could serve as proof, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of His Messenger.

Abu Bakr Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "The lowest of the people of Paradise in station is the one who is shown his gardens, his spouses, his blessings, his servants and his couches, extending a thousand years' journey. And the most honoured of them before Allah is the one who looks upon His Face morning and evening." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ ﴿looking at their Lord﴾.

Ahmad related in al-Musnad from the same narration, with the wording: "Indeed the most excellent of them in station will look upon the Face of Allah twice every day."

An-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni, who graded it sound, and Abu Nu'aym related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord? He said: Do you see the sun on a day with no cloud in it, and do you see the moon on a night with no cloud in it? We said: Yes. He said: Indeed you will see your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, until one of you is brought before his Lord in a face-to-face reckoning, and He says: 'My servant, do you recognise the sin of such and such?' He says: 'Did You not forgive me?' He says: 'By My forgiveness you have reached this.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 75, verses 1–25 (part 1 of 3):

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, through several chains, related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat al-Qiyamah" was revealed at Mecca. In one wording it is "Surat La Uqsimu."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "Surat La Uqsimu" was revealed at Mecca.

(p-1557)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. Abu ʿUbayda and a group of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the *la* (not) is superfluous, and the estimated reading is "I swear."

Al-Samarqandi said: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of ﴿la uqsimu﴾ is "uqsimu" (I swear). They differed over the explanation of the *la*. Some of them said: it is superfluous, and its superfluity is found in the speech of the Arabs, as in His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate," and ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I remembered Layla, and passion seized me,*
*and the core of my heart almost was cut, not cut.*

Others said: it is a rejection of their speech, in which they denied the resurrection, as if he said: "The matter is not as you mention. [I swear by the Day of Resurrection]." This is the view of al-Farra' and many of the grammarians, like the saying of one speaker: "No, by God," so *la* is a rejection of a statement that preceded it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*No, by your father, daughter of al-ʿAmiri,*
*the people do not claim that I flee.*

It was also said that it is for negation, but not a negation of the oath itself; rather, it negates what indicates the magnification and exaltation of the one sworn by. As if the meaning of "la uqsimu bi-kadhā" (I do not swear by such-and-such) is: I do not magnify it by swearing by it as it deserves to be magnified, for it deserves more than that.

It was also said that it is for negating the oath because the matter is clear. The discussion of this has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿So I do not swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 75].

Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir in one narration from him, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Hurmuz read *la-uqsimu* without the alif, on the basis that the *lam* is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). The first view is the most preferred of these views. Al-Razi objected to it with things that do not weaken its strength nor undermine its preponderance. God's swearing by the Day of Resurrection is for its glorification and exaltation, and God may swear by whatever of His creatures He wills.

﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾. Some people went to the view that He, glory be to Him, swore by the self-reproaching soul just as He swore by the Day of Resurrection, so the discussion about this *la* is like the discussion about the first one. This is the view of the majority.

Al-Hasan said: He swore by the Day of Resurrection and did not swear by the self-reproaching soul.

Al-Tha'labi said: The correct view is that He swore by both of them together. The meaning of "the self-reproaching soul" is the soul that blames its owner for his shortcoming, or that blames all souls for their shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: By God, it is the soul of the believer. You do not see the believer except that he blames himself: "What did I intend by such-and-such? What did I intend by such-and-such?" But the wicked does not rebuke his soul.

Mujahid said: It is the soul that blames for what has passed and regrets. It blames itself for evil: why did it do it? And for good: why did it not increase it? Al-Farra' said: There is no soul, whether righteous or wicked, except that it blames itself. If it has done good, it says: "If only I had done more." If it has done evil, it says: "If only I had not done it."

On this basis, the speech is coming in the manner of praise for the soul, so swearing by it is good and permissible.

It was also said that *al-lawwama* means "the one who is blamed and disgraced," so it is a description of blame. On this basis, whoever denied that it is an oath argued, since the soul of the disobedient has no worth by which one would swear.

Muqatil said: It is the soul of the unbeliever, which blames itself and grieves in the Hereafter over what it neglected regarding God's right. The first is preferable.

﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ The intended meaning of "man" is the species. It was said that "man" means the unbeliever. The *hamza* is for denial. *An* is the lightened form of the heavy (*an*), and its noun is a deleted pronoun of the matter. The meaning: Does man think that the matter is that We will not gather his bones after they have become dust, so that We would restore them as a new creation? That is a false supposition, for We gather them. What this statement indicates is the answer to the oath.

Al-Zajjaj said: I swear by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul that We will surely gather the bones for resurrection. This is the answer to the oath.

Al-Nahhas said: The answer to the oath is omitted, meaning: "He will surely resurrect," and the meaning is that God, glory be to Him, resurrects all the parts of man. He specified the bones because they are the mold of creation.

﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾. *Bala* is an affirmation of what follows the negation to which the interrogation is directed. Pausing on this word is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His saying *qadirina* (able). The accusative of *qadirina* is in the status of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Yes, We gather them, being able." So the state is from the implied verb's pronoun. It was also said the meaning is: "Yes, We gather them, estimating [ourselves] able."

Al-Farra' said: That is, We are able, and We are capable of more than that.

He also said: It is permissible to put it in the accusative by repetition, meaning: "Yes, let him reckon us able." It was also said the estimate is: "Yes, We were able."

Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *bala qadirun* (yes, [We] are able), on the estimate of a subject: that is, "Yes, We are able."

The meaning of ﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾ is: to join some of them to others, and return them as they were, despite their fineness and smallness. How then [would it be] with the large limbs? God, glory be to Him, drew attention with the *banan*, which is the fingers, to the rest of the limbs, and that the power to resurrect them and return them as they were is more fitting in power than returning the small, delicate fingers, which contain joints, nails, delicate veins, and fine bones. This is the reason for specifying them by mention. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba said this.

Most of the exegetes said: The meaning of the verse is that We would make the fingers of his hands and feet one thing, like the sole of a camel or the hoof of a donkey, a single plate without cracks in it, so he would not be able to benefit from them in delicate work such as writing, sewing, and the like. But We separated his fingers so that he may benefit by them.

It was also said the meaning is: Rather, We are able to return man in the form of beasts, so how much more in the form in which he was? The first is preferable. From it is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Death is subject to my hand, when I*
*join its fingertips with the Hindi sword.*

By *banan* he drew attention to the rest of the limbs.

﴿Rather, man desires to continue in sin ahead of him﴾. This is coordinated with "Does man think" either as an interrogation similar to it, turning away from the rebuke by that to the rebuke by this, or as an affirmation which has moved from interrogation.

The meaning: Rather, man desires to advance his wickedness among the times before him, and what time will come to him, so he advances the sin and delays repentance.

Ibn al-Anbari said: He desires to commit wickedness for as long as his life is extended, and it is not in his intention to turn back from a sin that he commits.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He says, "I will repent later," and does not repent until death comes to him while he is in his worst condition.

Al-Dahhak said: It is hope. He says, "I will live and enjoy some of the world," and does not mention death. *Fujur* (wickedness) originally means inclination away from the truth. It applies to everyone who inclines from the truth by speech or action. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He swore by God, Abu Hafs ʿUmar,*
*that no thorn-prick or thorn-scratch touched her. O God, forgive him if he was wicked.*

﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This sentence is a new statement explaining the meaning of "yafjur" (continues in sin). The meaning: he asks when the Day of Resurrection is, by way of asking with disbelief and mockery.

﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. That is: it is terrified and bewildered. From "barraqa al-rajul," when a man looks at lightning and his sight is stunned.

The majority read *bariqa* with a kasra on the *ra'*.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and al-Zajjaj and others said: the meaning is "bewildered, so he does not blink." From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Even if Luqman the wise were confronted*
*by a clear Mayy [a woman] before his eyes, he would almost be dazzled.*

Al-Khalil and al-Farra' said: *bariqa* with a kasra means: terrified, stunned, and bewildered. The Arabs say of the astonished person: "He has become *bariq*, so he is *bariq*." Al-Farra' recited:

*Tend your soul and do not weary me,*
*treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

That is: do not be terrified by the multitude of wounds that are on you.

Nafiʿ and Aban on the authority of ʿAsim read *baraqa* with a fatha on the *ra'*: that is, his sight shone from the intensity of its staring at death.

Mujahid and others said: This is at the time of death. It was said: *baraqa*, *yabraqu*, means he split his eyes open and kept them open.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The fatha and the kasra of the *ra'* are two dialects with the same meaning.

﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾. The majority read *khasafa* with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *sin*, in the active voice.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, and Abu Haywah read it with a damma on the *kha'* and a kasra on the *sin*, in the passive voice. The meaning of "khasafa al-qamar": its light has gone and does not return, as it returns when it is eclipsed in this world. It is said *khasafa* when all its light has gone, and *kasafa* when some of its light has gone.

﴿And the sun and moon are joined﴾: that is, their light has gone entirely. He did not say "joined" (feminine), because the feminine is metaphorical. Al-Mubarrad said this.

Abu ʿUbayda said: It is the predominance of the masculine over the feminine.

Al-Kisa'i said: It is treated according to the meaning of a collection of lights.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: He did not say "jumiʿat" because the meaning between them is in the going of their light. It was also said: He joined them in their rising from the west, both black, folded, and dark.

ʿAta' said: He will join them on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be thrown into the sea and become the great fire of God.

It was also said: The sun and the moon will be joined, so there will be no alternation of night and day there.

Ibn Masʿud read: "And the sun and the moon were joined."

﴿On that day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ That is: he says at the occurrence of these events, "Where is the escape?" *Al-mafarr* is a verbal noun in the sense of *al-firar* (flight).

Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that it is the place of flight. From it is the saying of the poet:

*Where is the escape, while the rams butt each other,*
*and every ram that flees from them is disgraced?*

Al-Mawardi said: It admits two meanings: first, where is the escape from God, glory be to Him, out of shame before Him? Second, where is the escape from Hell, out of fear of it?

The majority read ﴿ayna al-mafarr﴾ with a fatha on the *mim* and the *fa'*, as a verbal noun, as has already passed.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'*, as a noun of place: that is, where is the place of flight?

Al-Kisa'i said: They are two dialects, like *madabb* and *midabb*, and *masahh* and *misahh*. al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa'*, meaning by it the man who is good at fleeing. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Attacking, fleeing, advancing, retreating, together, like a boulder of rock that the torrent has cast down from a height.*

That is: good at fleeing and attacking.

﴿Never! There is no refuge﴾. That is: there is no mountain, no fortress, and no shelter from God.

Ibn Jubayr said: there is no escape and no protection.

*Al-wazar* in language is what a person takes refuge in: a fortress, a mountain, or other things. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*Bakr surely knows that we are the best in judgment and in the moment of fear, a refuge.*

Another said:

*By my life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age.*

Al-Suddi said: When they were frightened in the world they would take refuge in the mountains. So God said to them: "There is no refuge that will protect you from Me on that day." And *kalla* (never) is for rebuke, or for negating what preceded it, or with the meaning of "truly."

﴿To your Lord on that day is the resting place﴾. That is: the return, the end, and the destination, not to anything else. It was also said: To Him is the judgment among the servants, not to anything else. It was also said: *al-mustaqarr* is the settling where God settles them.

﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind﴾. That is: on the Day of Resurrection he will be informed of what good and evil he did.

Qatadah said: of the obedience he did, and the obedience he left and did not do.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: of what he sent ahead of his wealth and what he left to the heirs.

Mujahid said: of the first of his deeds and the last of them.

Al-Dahhak said: of the obligation he sent ahead and the obligation he left.

Al-Qushayri said: This informing will be on the Day of Resurrection at the weighing of deeds, and it may be at the time of death.

Al-Qurtubi said: The first is more apparent.

﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾. The *basirah* (witness, insight) is raised as the predicate of *al-insan*. *ʿAla nafsihi* (against himself) is connected to *basirah*.

Al-Akhfash said: He made it [the human being] himself the insight (baṣīrah), just as you say of a man, "You are a proof against yourself." It was also said that the meaning is that his limbs bear witness against him for what he did, as in His words: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. Al-Farra' recited:

*As if upon the man of intellect there is an eye that sees,*
*Observing his place, or a watcher who is looking.*

So the meaning is: rather, the human's limbs are witnesses against him.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Qutaybi said: This *hā'* in *baṣīrah* is what the grammarians call the *hā' al-mubālaghah* (the *hā'* of intensification), as in their saying *'allāmah* (very learned).

It was also said that *al-baṣīrah* refers to the two recording angels who write down whatever good and evil he does, and the *tā'* in that case is the feminine marker.

Al-Hasan said: That is, he is perceptive of the faults of his own self.

﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: that is, even if he makes excuses and argues on behalf of himself, that will not benefit him.

It is said *ma'dhirah* and *ma'ādhir* (pl.).

Al-Farra' said: That is, even if he makes excuses, there will be someone to deny his excuse.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ma'ādhir* means the veils (*al-sutūr*), and its singular is *mi'dhār*. That is: even if he lets down veils, wishing to hide himself, his own self is a witness against him. Thus said al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddi, and the veil in the dialect of Yemen is called *mi'dhār*. Thus said al-Mubarrad, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*But she [the dwelling] withheld for a while a place from us,*
*And she spent her day with veils (al-ma'ādhir).*

The first interpretation is the better one, and it was the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil. Similar to it is His words: ﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ [Ghafir: 52], and His words: ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], and the saying of the poet:

*It is not good that a man should excuse himself,*
*When among all the people there is no one to excuse him.*

﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to move his lips and tongue with the Qur'an when it was revealed to him, before Jibril had finished reciting the revelation, out of eagerness to memorize it (ﷺ). So this verse was revealed: that is, do not move your tongue with the Qur'an when the revelation is being delivered, in order to take it quickly, fearing that it might slip away from you. Similar to this is His words: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], and so on.

﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection﴾ in your breast, so that nothing of it is lost to you, ﴿and its recitation﴾, that is, the establishing of its recitation on your tongue.

Al-Farra' said: *al-qirā'ah* and *al-Qur'ān* are both verbal nouns (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: ﴿So follow its recitation﴾ means: follow its laws and rulings.

﴿So when We have recited it﴾, that is, when We have completed its recitation to you through the tongue of Jibril, ﴿then follow its recitation﴾, that is, its recitation.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾, that is, the explanation of what it contains of the lawful and the unlawful, and the clarifying of what is unclear in it.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that upon Us is that We send it down to you as an Arabic Qur'an, containing clarification for the people.

It was also said that the meaning is: indeed, it is upon Us that We make it clear through your tongue.

﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾. (*Kallā*) is for deterring from haste and for encouraging patience. It was also said that it is a deterrence for those who do not believe in the Qur'an and in its being clear, from among the disbelievers.

'Ata' said: That is, Abu Jahl does not believe in the Qur'an and its clarification.

The people of Medina and the Kufans recited ﴿Rather, you love﴾ and *tadharūna* (you leave) with the second-person form in both verbs. The rest recited with the third-person form in both. According to the first reading, the address is to them as rebuke and reproach. According to the second reading, the speech refers back to the human being, since it means "people." The meaning is: you love the world and leave the Hereafter, so you do not act for it.

﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾, that is, bright, fresh and beautiful. It is said: a tree that is *nāḍir* and a meadow that is *nāḍir*, meaning beautiful and luxuriant. The freshness of life is its beauty and delight.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators say: shining, luminous, bright.

﴿Looking at their Lord﴾. This is from looking (*naẓar*): that is, to their Creator and the Owner of their affair. *Nāẓirah*: that is, they look at Him. This is what the majority of the scholars said. What is meant by it is what the sound hadiths have transmitted in a widely transmitted way (*mutawātir*), that the servants will look upon their Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as they look at the moon on the night of the full moon.

Ibn Kathir said: And this, praise be to Allah, is agreed upon among the Companions, the Successors and the predecessors of this Ummah, just as it is agreed upon among the Imams of Islam and the guides of mankind.

Mujahid said: Here *naẓar* means waiting for the reward that they have with Allah. Something similar was narrated from 'Ikrimah.

It was said: this is not authentically reported except from Mujahid alone.

When someone says, "I looked at so-and-so," it is nothing but seeing with the eye. When they want to mean waiting, they say *naẓartuhu* (I awaited him), as in the words of the poet:

*Indeed, if you two would wait for me (tunẓirānī) for a while of time,*
*It would benefit me before Umm Jundab.*

When they want the sight of the eye, they say *naẓartu ilayhi* (I looked at him), as the poet said:

*I looked at her while the stars were like*
*Lamps of monks kindled for a feast.*

And the saying of another:

*Indeed I, when you promised me, am looking (nāẓir) to you*
*With the look of the poor man at the wealthy rich one.*

That is: I look at you with the look of humility, as the poor man looks at the rich man. The poetry and sayings of the Arabs on this are very numerous.

*Wujūh* (faces) is the subject (mubtada'), and it is permissible to begin with it though it is indefinite, because the context is one of detailing. *Nāḍirah* is an adjective of *wujūh*, and *yawma'idhin* (on that day) is an adverbial complement of *nāḍirah*. Even if the context were not one of detailing, the description of the indefinite by the phrase *nāḍirah* would make it permissible to begin with it. But the context of detailing by itself permits beginning with an indefinite noun.

﴿And faces on that Day will be gloomy﴾, that is, frowning, scowling, dejected.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: *basara al-rajul wajhahu busūran*, meaning he frowned.

Al-Suddi said: *bāsirah* means changed, and it was said: yellowed. The faces here refer to the faces of the disbelievers.

﴿They will think that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾. *Al-fāqirah* is the great catastrophe. It is said: *faqarahu al-fāqirah*, meaning it broke his spine.

Qatadah said: *al-fāqirah* is evil. Al-Suddi said: destruction. Ibn Zayd said: entering the Fire.

The origin of *al-fāqirah* is branding on the nose of a camel with an iron or fire until it reaches the bone. Thus said al-Asma'i. From this comes their saying, "He has worked on him the *fāqirah*."

Al-Nabighah said:

*Is there for me a grave that always stands before me,*
*And a blow of an axe above my head, a *fāqirah*?*

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His words: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1]. He said: Your Lord swears by whatever of His creation He wills. I said: ﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 2]. He said: the blameworthy self (*al-nafs al-la'ūm*). I said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3] ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 4]. He said: If He willed, He would make it a hoof or a claw.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: *al-lawwāmah* (the self-reproaching) means the blameworthy.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also: it is the one that blames for good and evil, saying, "If only I had done such and such."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also: it regrets what has passed and blames itself for it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also regarding ﴿But man wishes to continue in sin before him﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 5]: he said: it proceeds forward.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding the verse: he said: he is the disbeliever who denies the reckoning.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: he said: that is, the hope (*al-amal*). He says: I will act, then repent.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Amal* and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from him also regarding the verse: he said: he puts off repentance and delays it.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, (p. 1560) and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from him also: ﴿But man wishes to continue in sin before him﴾ he says: "I will repent later." ﴿He asks: when is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 6]. He said: he says, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" He said: So He explained to him: ﴿When the sight is dazzled﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 7]. Ibn Jarir transmitted from him: when the sight is dazzled, meaning death.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿No refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11]: he said: no fortress.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas through several chains regarding His words: ﴿No refuge﴾: he said: no fortress and no refuge. In one wording: no protection. In another wording: no mountain.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and kept back﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]: he said: what he sent forward of deeds, and what he kept back of a sunnah practiced after him, whether good or evil.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similar from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: what he sent forward of disobedience and what he kept back of obedience, and he will be informed of that.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through several chains from him regarding His words: ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 14]: he said: he bears witness against himself alone. ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: he said: even if he makes excuses.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾: he said: his hearing, his sight, his hands, his feet and his limbs. ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: he said: even if he strips off his clothes.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to suffer hardship in receiving the revelation, so he would move his tongue and lips with it, fearing that it would slip away from him, desiring to memorize it. So Allah revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17]. He said: It says: indeed upon Us is that We gather it in your breast, then you recite it. ﴿So when We have recited it﴾: it says: when We have sent it down to you. ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾: listen to it and be silent. ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾: that We explain it through your tongue. In another wording: upon Us is that We recite it. So after that, whenever Jibril came to him, he would lower his gaze (in another wording: listen), and when he left, he would recite it, just as Allah had promised him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: ﴿So when We have recited it﴾: he said: We have clarified it. ﴿Then follow its recitation﴾: he says: act upon it. 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾: he said: the world was hastened for them, its evil and its good, and the Hereafter was hidden from them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾: he said: luxuriant.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ajurri in *al-Shari'ah*, al-Lalika'i in *al-Sunnah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ru'yah* transmitted from him regarding ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾: he said: meaning their beauty. ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾: he said: they looked at the Creator.

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him: ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾: he said: they look at the face of their Lord.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas ibn Malik who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾ ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾, he said: They will look at their Lord without modality, without a bounded limit, and without a known attribute."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The people said: O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection? He said: Do you have any difficulty seeing the sun when there is no cloud beneath it? They said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said: Do you have any difficulty seeing the moon on the night of the full moon when there is no cloud beneath it? They said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said: Indeed you will see Him on the Day of Resurrection in the same way."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah.

We have already mentioned that the hadiths about the vision are widely transmitted, so we will not lengthen by citing them; they come in a separate work. Those who denied it and considered it far-fetched have not held onto anything that could serve as proof, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of His Messenger.

Abu Bakr Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "The lowest of the people of Paradise in station is the one who is shown his gardens, his spouses, his blessings, his servants and his couches, extending a thousand years' journey. And the most honoured of them before Allah is the one who looks upon His Face morning and evening." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ ﴿looking at their Lord﴾.

Ahmad related in al-Musnad from the same narration, with the wording: "Indeed the most excellent of them in station will look upon the Face of Allah twice every day."

An-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni, who graded it sound, and Abu Nu'aym related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord? He said: Do you see the sun on a day with no cloud in it, and do you see the moon on a night with no cloud in it? We said: Yes. He said: Indeed you will see your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, until one of you is brought before his Lord in a face-to-face reckoning, and He says: 'My servant, do you recognise the sin of such and such?' He says: 'Did You not forgive me?' He says: 'By My forgiveness you have reached this.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 75, verses 1–25 (part 1 of 3):

This surah is Meccan, without any dispute.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, through several chains, related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat al-Qiyamah" was revealed at Mecca. In one wording it is "Surat La Uqsimu."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "Surat La Uqsimu" was revealed at Mecca.

(p-1557)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. Abu ʿUbayda and a group of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the *la* (not) is superfluous, and the estimated reading is "I swear."

Al-Samarqandi said: The exegetes agreed that the meaning of ﴿la uqsimu﴾ is "uqsimu" (I swear). They differed over the explanation of the *la*. Some of them said: it is superfluous, and its superfluity is found in the speech of the Arabs, as in His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate," and ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I remembered Layla, and passion seized me,*
*and the core of my heart almost was cut, not cut.*

Others said: it is a rejection of their speech, in which they denied the resurrection, as if he said: "The matter is not as you mention. [I swear by the Day of Resurrection]." This is the view of al-Farra' and many of the grammarians, like the saying of one speaker: "No, by God," so *la* is a rejection of a statement that preceded it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*No, by your father, daughter of al-ʿAmiri,*
*the people do not claim that I flee.*

It was also said that it is for negation, but not a negation of the oath itself; rather, it negates what indicates the magnification and exaltation of the one sworn by. As if the meaning of "la uqsimu bi-kadhā" (I do not swear by such-and-such) is: I do not magnify it by swearing by it as it deserves to be magnified, for it deserves more than that.

It was also said that it is for negating the oath because the matter is clear. The discussion of this has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿So I do not swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 75].

Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir in one narration from him, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Hurmuz read *la-uqsimu* without the alif, on the basis that the *lam* is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'). The first view is the most preferred of these views. Al-Razi objected to it with things that do not weaken its strength nor undermine its preponderance. God's swearing by the Day of Resurrection is for its glorification and exaltation, and God may swear by whatever of His creatures He wills.

﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾. Some people went to the view that He, glory be to Him, swore by the self-reproaching soul just as He swore by the Day of Resurrection, so the discussion about this *la* is like the discussion about the first one. This is the view of the majority.

Al-Hasan said: He swore by the Day of Resurrection and did not swear by the self-reproaching soul.

Al-Tha'labi said: The correct view is that He swore by both of them together. The meaning of "the self-reproaching soul" is the soul that blames its owner for his shortcoming, or that blames all souls for their shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: By God, it is the soul of the believer. You do not see the believer except that he blames himself: "What did I intend by such-and-such? What did I intend by such-and-such?" But the wicked does not rebuke his soul.

Mujahid said: It is the soul that blames for what has passed and regrets. It blames itself for evil: why did it do it? And for good: why did it not increase it? Al-Farra' said: There is no soul, whether righteous or wicked, except that it blames itself. If it has done good, it says: "If only I had done more." If it has done evil, it says: "If only I had not done it."

On this basis, the speech is coming in the manner of praise for the soul, so swearing by it is good and permissible.

It was also said that *al-lawwama* means "the one who is blamed and disgraced," so it is a description of blame. On this basis, whoever denied that it is an oath argued, since the soul of the disobedient has no worth by which one would swear.

Muqatil said: It is the soul of the unbeliever, which blames itself and grieves in the Hereafter over what it neglected regarding God's right. The first is preferable.

﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ The intended meaning of "man" is the species. It was said that "man" means the unbeliever. The *hamza* is for denial. *An* is the lightened form of the heavy (*an*), and its noun is a deleted pronoun of the matter. The meaning: Does man think that the matter is that We will not gather his bones after they have become dust, so that We would restore them as a new creation? That is a false supposition, for We gather them. What this statement indicates is the answer to the oath.

Al-Zajjaj said: I swear by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul that We will surely gather the bones for resurrection. This is the answer to the oath.

Al-Nahhas said: The answer to the oath is omitted, meaning: "He will surely resurrect," and the meaning is that God, glory be to Him, resurrects all the parts of man. He specified the bones because they are the mold of creation.

﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾. *Bala* is an affirmation of what follows the negation to which the interrogation is directed. Pausing on this word is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His saying *qadirina* (able). The accusative of *qadirina* is in the status of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Yes, We gather them, being able." So the state is from the implied verb's pronoun. It was also said the meaning is: "Yes, We gather them, estimating [ourselves] able."

Al-Farra' said: That is, We are able, and We are capable of more than that.

He also said: It is permissible to put it in the accusative by repetition, meaning: "Yes, let him reckon us able." It was also said the estimate is: "Yes, We were able."

Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *bala qadirun* (yes, [We] are able), on the estimate of a subject: that is, "Yes, We are able."

The meaning of ﴿to put together even his fingertips﴾ is: to join some of them to others, and return them as they were, despite their fineness and smallness. How then [would it be] with the large limbs? God, glory be to Him, drew attention with the *banan*, which is the fingers, to the rest of the limbs, and that the power to resurrect them and return them as they were is more fitting in power than returning the small, delicate fingers, which contain joints, nails, delicate veins, and fine bones. This is the reason for specifying them by mention. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba said this.

Most of the exegetes said: The meaning of the verse is that We would make the fingers of his hands and feet one thing, like the sole of a camel or the hoof of a donkey, a single plate without cracks in it, so he would not be able to benefit from them in delicate work such as writing, sewing, and the like. But We separated his fingers so that he may benefit by them.

It was also said the meaning is: Rather, We are able to return man in the form of beasts, so how much more in the form in which he was? The first is preferable. From it is the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Death is subject to my hand, when I*
*join its fingertips with the Hindi sword.*

By *banan* he drew attention to the rest of the limbs.

﴿Rather, man desires to continue in sin ahead of him﴾. This is coordinated with "Does man think" either as an interrogation similar to it, turning away from the rebuke by that to the rebuke by this, or as an affirmation which has moved from interrogation.

The meaning: Rather, man desires to advance his wickedness among the times before him, and what time will come to him, so he advances the sin and delays repentance.

Ibn al-Anbari said: He desires to commit wickedness for as long as his life is extended, and it is not in his intention to turn back from a sin that he commits.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He says, "I will repent later," and does not repent until death comes to him while he is in his worst condition.

Al-Dahhak said: It is hope. He says, "I will live and enjoy some of the world," and does not mention death. *Fujur* (wickedness) originally means inclination away from the truth. It applies to everyone who inclines from the truth by speech or action. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He swore by God, Abu Hafs ʿUmar,*
*that no thorn-prick or thorn-scratch touched her. O God, forgive him if he was wicked.*

﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This sentence is a new statement explaining the meaning of "yafjur" (continues in sin). The meaning: he asks when the Day of Resurrection is, by way of asking with disbelief and mockery.

﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾. That is: it is terrified and bewildered. From "barraqa al-rajul," when a man looks at lightning and his sight is stunned.

The majority read *bariqa* with a kasra on the *ra'*.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and al-Zajjaj and others said: the meaning is "bewildered, so he does not blink." From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Even if Luqman the wise were confronted*
*by a clear Mayy [a woman] before his eyes, he would almost be dazzled.*

Al-Khalil and al-Farra' said: *bariqa* with a kasra means: terrified, stunned, and bewildered. The Arabs say of the astonished person: "He has become *bariq*, so he is *bariq*." Al-Farra' recited:

*Tend your soul and do not weary me,*
*treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

That is: do not be terrified by the multitude of wounds that are on you.

Nafiʿ and Aban on the authority of ʿAsim read *baraqa* with a fatha on the *ra'*: that is, his sight shone from the intensity of its staring at death.

Mujahid and others said: This is at the time of death. It was said: *baraqa*, *yabraqu*, means he split his eyes open and kept them open.

Abu ʿUbayda said: The fatha and the kasra of the *ra'* are two dialects with the same meaning.

﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾. The majority read *khasafa* with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *sin*, in the active voice.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, and Abu Haywah read it with a damma on the *kha'* and a kasra on the *sin*, in the passive voice. The meaning of "khasafa al-qamar": its light has gone and does not return, as it returns when it is eclipsed in this world. It is said *khasafa* when all its light has gone, and *kasafa* when some of its light has gone.

﴿And the sun and moon are joined﴾: that is, their light has gone entirely. He did not say "joined" (feminine), because the feminine is metaphorical. Al-Mubarrad said this.

Abu ʿUbayda said: It is the predominance of the masculine over the feminine.

Al-Kisa'i said: It is treated according to the meaning of a collection of lights.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: He did not say "jumiʿat" because the meaning between them is in the going of their light. It was also said: He joined them in their rising from the west, both black, folded, and dark.

ʿAta' said: He will join them on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be thrown into the sea and become the great fire of God.

It was also said: The sun and the moon will be joined, so there will be no alternation of night and day there.

Ibn Masʿud read: "And the sun and the moon were joined."

﴿On that day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ That is: he says at the occurrence of these events, "Where is the escape?" *Al-mafarr* is a verbal noun in the sense of *al-firar* (flight).

Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that it is the place of flight. From it is the saying of the poet:

*Where is the escape, while the rams butt each other,*
*and every ram that flees from them is disgraced?*

Al-Mawardi said: It admits two meanings: first, where is the escape from God, glory be to Him, out of shame before Him? Second, where is the escape from Hell, out of fear of it?

The majority read ﴿ayna al-mafarr﴾ with a fatha on the *mim* and the *fa'*, as a verbal noun, as has already passed.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa'*, as a noun of place: that is, where is the place of flight?

Al-Kisa'i said: They are two dialects, like *madabb* and *midabb*, and *masahh* and *misahh*. al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa'*, meaning by it the man who is good at fleeing. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Attacking, fleeing, advancing, retreating, together, like a boulder of rock that the torrent has cast down from a height.*

That is: good at fleeing and attacking.

﴿Never! There is no refuge﴾. That is: there is no mountain, no fortress, and no shelter from God.

Ibn Jubayr said: there is no escape and no protection.

*Al-wazar* in language is what a person takes refuge in: a fortress, a mountain, or other things. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*Bakr surely knows that we are the best in judgment and in the moment of fear, a refuge.*

Another said:

*By my life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age.*

Al-Suddi said: When they were frightened in the world they would take refuge in the mountains. So God said to them: "There is no refuge that will protect you from Me on that day." And *kalla* (never) is for rebuke, or for negating what preceded it, or with the meaning of "truly."

﴿To your Lord on that day is the resting place﴾. That is: the return, the end, and the destination, not to anything else. It was also said: To Him is the judgment among the servants, not to anything else. It was also said: *al-mustaqarr* is the settling where God settles them.

﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind﴾. That is: on the Day of Resurrection he will be informed of what good and evil he did.

Qatadah said: of the obedience he did, and the obedience he left and did not do.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: of what he sent ahead of his wealth and what he left to the heirs.

Mujahid said: of the first of his deeds and the last of them.

Al-Dahhak said: of the obligation he sent ahead and the obligation he left.

Al-Qushayri said: This informing will be on the Day of Resurrection at the weighing of deeds, and it may be at the time of death.

Al-Qurtubi said: The first is more apparent.

﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself﴾. The *basirah* (witness, insight) is raised as the predicate of *al-insan*. *ʿAla nafsihi* (against himself) is connected to *basirah*.

Al-Akhfash said: He made it [the human being] himself the insight (baṣīrah), just as you say of a man, "You are a proof against yourself." It was also said that the meaning is that his limbs bear witness against him for what he did, as in His words: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. Al-Farra' recited:

*As if upon the man of intellect there is an eye that sees,*
*Observing his place, or a watcher who is looking.*

So the meaning is: rather, the human's limbs are witnesses against him.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Qutaybi said: This *hā'* in *baṣīrah* is what the grammarians call the *hā' al-mubālaghah* (the *hā'* of intensification), as in their saying *'allāmah* (very learned).

It was also said that *al-baṣīrah* refers to the two recording angels who write down whatever good and evil he does, and the *tā'* in that case is the feminine marker.

Al-Hasan said: That is, he is perceptive of the faults of his own self.

﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾: that is, even if he makes excuses and argues on behalf of himself, that will not benefit him.

It is said *ma'dhirah* and *ma'ādhir* (pl.).

Al-Farra' said: That is, even if he makes excuses, there will be someone to deny his excuse.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ma'ādhir* means the veils (*al-sutūr*), and its singular is *mi'dhār*. That is: even if he lets down veils, wishing to hide himself, his own self is a witness against him. Thus said al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddi, and the veil in the dialect of Yemen is called *mi'dhār*. Thus said al-Mubarrad, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*But she [the dwelling] withheld for a while a place from us,*
*And she spent her day with veils (al-ma'ādhir).*

The first interpretation is the better one, and it was the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil. Similar to it is His words: ﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ [Ghafir: 52], and His words: ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], and the saying of the poet:

*It is not good that a man should excuse himself,*
*When among all the people there is no one to excuse him.*

﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to move his lips and tongue with the Qur'an when it was revealed to him, before Jibril had finished reciting the revelation, out of eagerness to memorize it (ﷺ). So this verse was revealed: that is, do not move your tongue with the Qur'an when the revelation is being delivered, in order to take it quickly, fearing that it might slip away from you. Similar to this is His words: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114], and so on.

﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection﴾ in your breast, so that nothing of it is lost to you, ﴿and its recitation﴾, that is, the establishing of its recitation on your tongue.

Al-Farra' said: *al-qirā'ah* and *al-Qur'ān* are both verbal nouns (maṣdar).

Qatadah said: ﴿So follow its recitation﴾ means: follow its laws and rulings.

﴿So when We have recited it﴾, that is, when We have completed its recitation to you through the tongue of Jibril, ﴿then follow its recitation﴾, that is, its recitation.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾, that is, the explanation of what it contains of the lawful and the unlawful, and the clarifying of what is unclear in it.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that upon Us is that We send it down to you as an Arabic Qur'an, containing clarification for the people.

It was also said that the meaning is: indeed, it is upon Us that We make it clear through your tongue.

﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾. (*Kallā*) is for deterring from haste and for encouraging patience. It was also said that it is a deterrence for those who do not believe in the Qur'an and in its being clear, from among the disbelievers.

'Ata' said: That is, Abu Jahl does not believe in the Qur'an and its clarification.

The people of Medina and the Kufans recited ﴿Rather, you love﴾ and *tadharūna* (you leave) with the second-person form in both verbs. The rest recited with the third-person form in both. According to the first reading, the address is to them as rebuke and reproach. According to the second reading, the speech refers back to the human being, since it means "people." The meaning is: you love the world and leave the Hereafter, so you do not act for it.

﴿Faces on that Day will be radiant﴾, that is, bright, fresh and beautiful. It is said: a tree that is *nāḍir* and a meadow that is *nāḍir*, meaning beautiful and luxuriant. The freshness of life is its beauty and delight.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators say: shining, luminous, bright.

﴿Looking at their Lord﴾. This is from looking (*naẓar*): that is, to their Creator and the Owner of their affair. *Nāẓirah*: that is, they look at Him. This is what the majority of the scholars said. What is meant by it is what the sound hadiths have transmitted in a widely transmitted way (*mutawātir*), that the servants will look upon their Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as they look at the moon on the night of the full moon.
